newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's liberals vow unity, divisions remain.
newsitem.headline: Russia's liberals vow unity, divisions remain.

text.p: Russia's fractious democrats pledged a new era of unity and cooperation on Monday, but they failed to bury completely the divisions that have bedevilled them since the fall of Soviet communism five years ago.

Led by former acting prime minister Yegor Gaidar, architect of Russia's early market reforms, seven liberal parties agreed to form a coalition aimed at boosting their joint appeal in a country better known for its authoritarian traditions.

"We have yet to determine how precisely we shall work together and take decisions. This coalition will not be a single organisation but rather a confederation of parties and movements that share liberal values," Gaidar told a news conference.
These values, outlined in a joint declaration, entail the creation of a free civil society based on individual rights as a buttress against the return of totalitarian rule.
The alliance is a clear attempt by Gaidar and other parties to assume a new image -- liberal rather than democratic -- after all of them lost parliamentary elections in December.
It is also a bid to win back the leading role in the liberal camp from Gaidar's rival Grigory Yavlinsky.
President Boris Yeltsin, once a champion of the liberal cause, has long since purged reformers like Gaidar from his team, usually in a bid to appease opposition in parliament.

The only prominent liberal from Gaidar's team remaining in the higher echelons of power is Anatoly Chubais, appointed president's chief of staff following Yeltsin's re-election in June for a second four-year term.
Despite the democrats' political weakness, however, Gaidar held out little prospect of Yavlinsky joining the new coalition.
"Yavlinksy's Yabolko (Apple) is a social democratic party and we are liberals," said Gaidar.

Yavlinksy, a feisty former economic adviser to Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev, took fourth place in the first round of Russia's presidential election in June with just over seven percent of the vote.
His Yabolko is the biggest democratic alliance in the State Duma lower house of parliament and the fourth largest faction.

Apart from personal antipathy, Gaidar -- who heads the Democratic Choice of Russia party -- has more radical views on economic reform than Yavlinsky, who lays stress on boosting investment and economic growth.
"There are fundamental differences between (our new coalition and Yavlinsky's party), not just personal ones," said Gaidar ally Galina Starovoitova of the Democratic Russia Party.
The signatory parties would cooperate in regional and local elections now taking place across the huge country, she said.
She estimated the current combined strength of the seven coalition members in the Duma at around 25 out of 450.
Irina Hakamada, another of the accord's signatories, said "not less than 17 percent" of Russian voters professed liberal values and deserved more effective political representation.
"We must show that a liberal alternative to socialism and to bureaucratic capitalism exists and is essential," she said.
Both Gaidar and Yavlinksy have been critical of Yeltsin's domestic and foreign policies, especially the brutal military campaign against separatists in Russia's southern breakaway region of Chechnya.
"We (liberals) are also opposed to the level of criminality and corruption in the current government," said Starovoitova.

"The president does not promote enough democrats but favours the old nomenklatura, mostly from Our Home is Russia party (of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin), that he nominates as regional governors and to other posts," she said.
